So he casts himself before Him, surrenders the whole matter to Him, and lays himself down before Him as a weak slave lays himself before a mighty, dominant king, who has full authority over his servant to do whatever He wills, while the servant has no authority over anything in any way. Then he finds rest from worries, griefs, distresses, regrets and sorrows. He entrusts all his needs and interests to the One who does not care about bearing them, who is not burdened by them and is not troubled by them. So He takes charge of them for him, and shows him His gentleness, kindness, mercy and benevolence in them, without weariness on the servant's part, without exhaustion, and without the servant's anxiety, because he has turned all his concern toward Him and made Him alone his aim. Thus He removes from him concern for his needs and worldly interests and empties his heart of them. How pleasant then is his life, how content his heart, and how great his joy and happiness.

If, however, he refuses except to manage himself and choose for himself, and concerns himself with his own portion rather than the right of his Lord, then He leaves him to what he has chosen and entrusts him to what he has taken on. Then there come upon him worry, grief, sorrow, distress, fear, weariness, a troubled mind and a bad state. No heart becomes clear, no deed is purified, no hope is attained, no rest is gained, and no pleasure can be enjoyed with it. Rather, indeed, he has been prevented from his happiness, his joy and the coolness of his eye. He toils in this world like a wild beast, gains nothing of hope from it, and does not take from it provision for the return.

Allah, glory be to Him, commanded the servant with a command and guaranteed him a guarantee. If he stands by His command with sincere counsel, truthfulness, sincerity and striving, then Allah, glory be to Him, stands by him with what He has guaranteed him: provision, sufficiency, victory and the fulfilment of needs. He, glory be to Him, guaranteed provision to whoever worships Him, victory to whoever relies upon Him and seeks help from Him, sufficiency to whoever makes Him his concern and aim, forgiveness to whoever asks Him for it, and the fulfilment of needs to whoever is sincere in asking for them, trusts in Him, and whose hope and desire for His bounty and generosity are strong. So the intelligent and discerning person concerns himself only with carrying out His command, establishing it and fulfilling it, not with His guarantee, for He is the Faithful, the Truthful, and who is more faithful to his covenant than Allah? Therefore, among the signs of happiness is turning one's concern toward the command of Allah rather than His guarantee. Among the signs of deprivation is a heart empty of concern for His command, of love for Him, of fear of Him, while being preoccupied with His guarantee. And Allah is the One whose help is sought.

Bishr ibn al-Harith said: "The people of the Hereafter are three: the worshipper, the ascetic, and the siddiq (the truthful, sincerely devoted one)."

The worshipper worships Allah while still attached to worldly ties; the ascetic worships Him by abandoning those ties; and the siddiq worships Him through contentment and conformity [with Him].

If He sees him take the world, he takes it; if He sees him leave it, he leaves it.

When Allah and His Messenger are on one side, beware of being on the other side, for that leads to opposition (mushaqqa) and hostility (muhadda). This is its root, and from it the word is derived. Opposition (mushaqqa) means being on one side while the one who opposes him is on another side, and hostility (muhadda) means being on one limit while he is on another limit. Do not consider this a small matter, for its beginnings lead to its end, and its little draws to its much. Be on the side where Allah and His Messenger are, even if all the people are on the other side, for there are consequences to this that are the most praiseworthy and the best of outcomes. For the servant there is nothing more beneficial to him in his worldly life, before his Hereafter. Most of creation are on the other side, especially when desire and fear grow strong. In such a situation you will hardly find anyone on the side where Allah and His Messenger are. Rather, people regard him as deficient in intellect and poor in choosing for himself, and sometimes they attribute madness to him. This is an inheritance from the enemies of the Messengers, for they attributed madness to them when they were on one side and the people were on another side.

But whoever settles himself upon this needs firm knowledge of what the Messenger brought, a certainty in his heart with no doubt in it, and complete patience in the face of those who oppose him and the blame of those who reproach him. This cannot be accomplished except with a strong desire for Allah, the Abode and the Hereafter, to the extent that the Hereafter becomes dearer to him than this world and more preferred by him than it, and Allah and His Messenger become dearer to him than anything else. There is nothing harder for a person than this at the beginning of the matter, for his self, his desire, his nature, his devil, his brothers and his companions from that other side call him to what is immediate. When he opposes them, they take up arms against him. If he is patient and steadfast, the help of Allah comes to him, that difficulty becomes easy, and that pain becomes pleasure. For the Lord is Most Appreciative, so He will certainly let him taste the pleasure of withdrawing to Allah and His Messenger, and show him the honour of that, so his joy and happiness increase, his heart rejoices, and he attains strength, delight and gladness. And those who were fighting him over this remain between one who fears him, one who makes peace with him, one who supports him, and one who abandons him. His army grows stronger and the army of the enemy grows weaker. Do not find opposing the people and withdrawing to Allah and His Messenger difficult, even if you are alone, for Allah is with you, you are under His watch, His protection and His safeguarding. Your certainty and patience are only being tested. The greatest helpers for you, after Allah's help, are with this: by the help of Allah, detachment from greed and fear. When you are detached from both, withdrawing to Allah and His Messenger becomes easy for you, and you will always be on the side where Allah and His Messenger are. But whenever greed takes hold of you, do not hope for this matter and do not let your soul entertain it.

If you say: "By what means can I be helped to be detached from greed and from fear?"

I say: By tawhid (monotheism), tawakkul (reliance), trust in Allah, and your knowledge that no one brings good deeds except Him, no one takes away evil deeds except Him, and that the whole matter belongs to Allah, and no one has anything alongside Allah.

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on Surah 28, verses 71–72:

God, glorified is He, singled out the day for the mention of sight, because it is its locus, and in it lies the authority of sight and its activity.

He singled out the night for the mention of hearing, because the authority of hearing is exercised at night, and animals hear at night what they do not hear during the day, since it is a time of quiet sounds, stilled movements, the strength of the authority of hearing, and the weakness of the authority of sight. The day is the reverse: in it is the strength of the authority of sight and the weakness of the authority of hearing.

So His saying, "Will you not then hear?" refers back to His saying, "Say: Have you considered? If God made the night perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what god other than God could bring you light?"

And His saying, "Will you not then see?" refers back to His saying, "Say: Have you considered? If God made the day perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection..."

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 28, verse 76:

So joy, when it is for the sake of Allah and for what Allah has bestowed, accompanied by fear and caution, does not harm its possessor; but when it is free of that, it will inevitably harm him.

And the people of Qarun said to him: ﴿Do not exult. Indeed, Allah does not like the exultant.﴾

(Section)

Know that what the people of this world gather of it is not a place for joy, because it is exposed to calamities, swift to vanish, grave in its outcome, and it is like a phantom of a dream that visited the lovesick one in sleep. Then the sleep ended, the phantom departed, and its visit was followed by separation.

Joy has come in the Qur'an in two kinds: unrestricted (mutlaq) and restricted (muqayyad).

The unrestricted kind has come in censure, such as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do not exult. Indeed, Allah does not like the exultant.﴾ [al-Qasas: 76] And His saying: ﴿Indeed, he is exultant and boastful.﴾ [Hud: 10]

The restricted kind is also of two types. The first is restricted to worldly things, causing its possessor to forget the grace and favour of Allah; this is blameworthy, such as His saying: ﴿Until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and at once they were in despair.﴾ [al-An'am: 44]

The second is restricted to the grace of Allah and His mercy. This too is of two types:

Grace and mercy as a means (sabab), and grace as a result (musabbab). The first is like His saying: ﴿Say: "By the grace of Allah and His mercy, let them rejoice; it is better than what they accumulate."﴾ [Yunus: 58]

The second is like His saying: ﴿Rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 170]

(Fa'ida / Lateefa)

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿And do good as Allah has done good to you﴾.

There is no doubt that no one can do good to the extent that Allah has done good to him, and what is intended is the essence of goodness, not its measure.

(Fa'ida)

The knower ('arif) does not command people to abandon this world, for they are not able to leave it. Rather, he commands them to abandon sins while they remain attached to their worldly life. Abandoning the world is a virtue, and abandoning sins is an obligation, so how can one who has not fulfilled the obligation be commanded to the virtue? If abandoning sins is difficult for them, then strive to make Allah beloved to them by mentioning His bounties, His favour, His goodness, the attributes of His perfection, and the descriptions of His majesty, for hearts are created with the disposition to love Him. When they become attached to His love, abandoning sins becomes easy for them, as do disregarding them, and persisting in them.

Yahya ibn Mu'adh said: "The intelligent person's pursuit of the world is better than the ignorant person's abandonment of it. The knower calls people to Allah through their worldly life, so responding is easy for them; the ascetic calls them to Allah by abandoning the world, so responding is hard for them. Weaning from the breast, which a person was attached to before he even knew himself, is severe, but it is better with the best and most virtuous of wet-nurses, for milk has an effect on the nature of the nursling, and nursing from a foolish woman returns with the foolishness of the child. The most beneficial nursing is that which comes from hunger. If you can endure the bitterness of weaning, well and good; otherwise, nurse in measure, for there is a surfeit that kills."

(Fasl)

The highest goal depends for its attainment on a lofty aspiration (himma) and a sound intention (niyya). Whoever lacks them is unable to reach it. When aspiration is lofty, it attaches itself to Him alone and not to anything else; when intention is sound, the servant takes the path that leads to Him. Intention makes the path singular for him, and aspiration makes the objective singular for him. When his objective and the path leading to it are unified, arrival is his ultimate end.

When aspiration is base, it attaches itself to base things and does not attach itself to the highest goal; when intention is not sound, his path does not lead to Him. Thus the matter revolves around the servant's aspiration and intention, and these two are his objective.

This is not completed for him except by abandoning three things: customs, traditions and conventions that people have invented.

Second: forsaking the obstacles (awa'iq) that hinder him from devoting himself to his objective and his path, and cutting them off.

Third: severing the attachments of the heart ( 'ala'iq) that come between him and singling out his attachment to the objective.

The difference between them is that obstacles are external occurrences, while attachments are inward attachments of the heart to permissible things and the like.

The root of this is abandoning superfluities that distract from the goal: food, drink, sleep and mixing with people. He takes from these what helps him in his pursuit and rejects what cuts him off from it or weakens his pursuit. And Allah is the One whose help is sought.

(Mawi'iza)

The Prophet (ﷺ) once addressed his companions. When the sun was on the tops of the mountains, at sunset, he said:

"Indeed, what remains of this world of what has passed is only like what remains of your day of this today of what has passed of it."

Let the intelligent person who counsels himself reflect upon this hadith, and let him know what he has gained from this time that remains in the whole world, so that he knows he is in delusion and confused dreams, and that he has sold eternal happiness and everlasting bliss for a base share that is worth nothing. Had he sought Allah, the Exalted, and the Hereafter, He would have given him that share in abundance and more.

As in some reports: "Son of Adam, sell the world for the Hereafter and you will profit from both; do not sell the Hereafter for the world and you will lose both."

Some of the early generations (salaf) said: "Son of Adam, you need your share of this world, but you need your share of the Hereafter even more. If you begin with your share of the world, you lose your share of the Hereafter and your share of the world is at risk. If you begin with your share of the Hereafter, you attain your share of the world, arranged in perfect order."

'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz (may Allah be pleased with him) used to say in his sermon: "O people, you were not created in vain, nor left neglected. You have a return in which Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, will gather you for judgement among you and decision between you. Lost and wretched is the servant whom Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has expelled from His mercy, which encompasses all things, and from His Garden whose width is the heavens and the earth.

Security tomorrow belongs only to those who fear Allah and are mindful of Him, who sold little for much, the transient for the everlasting, and wretchedness for happiness.

Do you not see that you are in the loins of those who perished, and that those who remain will succeed you?

Do you not see that every day you accompany one who goes out and returns to Allah, having fulfilled his term, his hope cut off, and you place him in a crevice of the earth, unsupported and unprepared, having shed his means, separated from his loved ones, and confronted with the reckoning?"

The point is that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has granted the servant, in this brief span, troops, numbers and reinforcements, and has shown him by what he may protect himself from his enemy, and by what he may free himself if taken captive.

(Nasiha)

Come, enter into the presence of Allah and dwell near Him in the Abode of Peace, without toil, fatigue or hardship, rather by one of the nearest and easiest paths. This is because you are in a moment between two times, which in reality is your life, your present time, between what has passed and what is yet to come. What has passed, you set right through repentance, regret and seeking forgiveness, and that is a matter with no toil, weariness or hardship upon you; it is an action of the heart, not a burdensome labour of the limbs. Your refraining from sins in the future is abstention and rest, not a deed of the limbs whose effort would be burdensome; it is resolve and a firm intention that refreshes your body, heart and inner self. So what has passed you set right by repentance, and what is to come you set right by abstention, resolve and intention. The limbs have no toil in these two. But the matter lies in your life, which is your time between the two times. If you waste it, you waste your happiness and salvation; if you preserve it while also setting right the two times before and after it with what I have mentioned, you are saved and gain rest, pleasure and bliss. Preserving it is harder than setting right what is before and after it, for preserving it means obliging yourself to what is most fitting and beneficial for you and greatest in attaining your happiness. In this, people differ enormously. By Allah, it is your days that have passed, in which you gather provision for your return, either to Paradise or to the Fire. If you take a path to your Lord through them, you attain the supreme happiness and the greatest success in this brief span, which has no proportion to eternity. If you prefer desires, comforts, amusement and play, they will pass from you quickly and leave you with a great, lasting pain, whose endurance is harder, more difficult and more lasting than the endurance of patience in refraining from what Allah has forbidden, persevering in His obedience, and opposing desire for His sake.

**(Section)**

The cause of abandonment (*khudhlan*, divine abandonment, that is, God withdrawing His support from a person) is that the recipient is not suitable, not fit, and not receptive to blessing. If blessings came to him, he would say, "This is mine, and I was only given it because I am worthy of it and deserve it," as God the Exalted said: ﴿He said, "I was only given it on account of knowledge I have."﴾

That is, "on knowledge I possess, by which I deserve it, merit it, and am fit for it."

Al-Farra' said: "i.e., on account of merit I have, since I was worthy of it and deserving of it when it was given to me."

Muqatil said: "He says, 'on the best knowledge of God that I have.'"

Abdullah ibn al-Harith ibn Nawfal mentioned Sulayman ibn Dawud regarding what he was given of kingship, then recited God's words: ﴿This is of the bounty of my Lord, to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful.﴾ He did not say, "This is because of my honour." Then he mentioned Qarun and his saying: ﴿I was only given it on knowledge I have.﴾

The meaning is that Sulayman saw what he was given as a bounty and favour from God upon him, and that he was tested by it through gratitude, whereas Qarun saw it as coming from himself and from his own deservingness.

Likewise is His saying, glorified be He: ﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us after hardship had touched him, he would surely say, "This is mine."﴾ That is, "I am worthy of it and deserving of it, so my possession of it is like the possession of an owner over his property." The believer sees it as a dominion belonging to his Lord and a favour from Him, bestowed on His servant without the servant having any right to it, but rather as a charity God gave him, when He had the right to withhold it. If He had withheld it, He would not have withheld anything that was owed to him. So when he does not witness this, and sees himself as worthy and deserving, his self makes him proud, he becomes arrogant with the blessing, exalts himself over it, and feels superior to others. So his share of it becomes joy and boasting, as He said, the Exalted: ﴿And if We let man taste mercy from Us, then We take it away from him, indeed he is despairing and ungrateful. And if We let him taste blessing after hardship has touched him, he will surely say, "The evils have gone from me." Indeed he is exultant and boastful.﴾

So He censured him for despair and disbelief at the time of testing by hardship, and for exultation and boasting at the time of trial by blessings. When the hardship was removed from him, he replaced the praise of God, His gratitude, and thanksgiving to Him with his saying, "The evils have gone from me." Had he said, "God removed the evils from me by His mercy and bounty," he would not have been censured for it; rather he would have been praised for it. But he was heedless of the Benefactor who removed them and attributed their departure to himself, so he rejoiced and boasted. When God, glorified be He, knows this from a servant's heart, it is among the greatest causes of that servant's abandonment and God's forsaking of him, for his place does not suit absolute and complete blessing. As He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed the worst of creatures in the sight of God are the deaf and the dumb who do not reason. And if God had known any good in them, He would have made them hear. And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while being averse.﴾

Thus He informed, glorified be He, that their place does not accept His blessing. Alongside this non-acceptance there is another obstacle preventing it from reaching them, namely their turning away and aversion once they know and recognize it.

It should be known that the causes of abandonment are the self remaining as it was originally created, left to itself, neglected and abandoned. So the causes of abandonment come from it and within it. The causes of success (*tawfiq*) are that God, glorified be He, made them receptive to blessing. So the causes of success come from Him and from His bounty, and He is the Creator of both, just as He created parts of the earth: this part is receptive to plants and that part is not receptive to them; and He created trees, some of which accept fruit and some of which do not; and He created the bee receptive to bringing forth from its bellies a drink of varying colours, while the wasp is not receptive to that; and He created good spirits receptive to His remembrance, His thanks, His proof, His majesty, His glorification, His oneness, and advising His servants, while He created wicked spirits not receptive to that, but rather to its opposite. He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing.

**[Section: On expressions the Prophet (ﷺ) disliked being said]**

Among them: that one says, "My soul became foul," or "My soul surged." Rather, let him say, "*laqisat*" (my soul became sickened).

Among them: calling the grapevine a *karm*. He forbade this and said, "Do not say *al-karm*; rather say *al-'inab* and *al-habalah*."

He disliked that a man should say, "The people have perished."

He said: "If he says that, then he is the most ruined of them." In the same sense: "The people have corrupted," "The times have corrupted," and the like.

He forbade saying, "What God wills and so-and-so wills." Rather, say, "What God wills, then so-and-so wills." A man said to him, "What God wills and you will." He said, "Have you made me a rival to God? Say: what God alone wills."

In the same sense: "Were it not for God and so-and-so, such-and-such would not have happened." This is even uglier and more objectionable. Likewise: "I am with God and with so-and-so," "I seek refuge in God and in so-and-so," "I am under the protection of God and of so-and-so," "I rely on God and on so-and-so." The one who says this has made so-and-so a rival to God, the Mighty and Majestic.

Among them: saying, "We were given rain by such-and-such a star (*nawʾ*, a lunar mansion)." Rather, say, "We were given rain by God's bounty and mercy."

Among them: swearing by other than God. It is authentically reported from him (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever swears by other than God has committed shirk (associating partners with God)."

Among them: saying in one's oath, "He is a Jew, or a Christian, or an unbeliever, if he does such-and-such."

Among them: saying to a Muslim, "O unbeliever!"

Among them: saying to the sultan (ruler), "King of kings." By analogy, "Judge of judges."

Among them: a master saying to his male or female slave, "My slave" or "My female slave," and a slave saying to his master, "My lord." Rather, the master should say, "My young man (*fata*) and my young woman (*fataty*)," and the slave should say, "My master" and "My mistress."

Among them: cursing the wind when it blows. Rather, one should ask God for its good and the good of what it was sent with, and seek refuge in God from its evil and the evil of what it was sent with.

Among them: cursing fever. He forbade this and said: "It removes the sins of the children of Adam as the furnace removes the dross of iron."

Among them: the prohibition of cursing the rooster. It is authentically reported from him (ﷺ) that he said: "Do not curse the rooster, for it wakes one for prayer."

Among them: calling out with the slogans of the *Jahiliyyah* (pre-Islamic ignorance), and taking pride in their pride, such as calling to tribes and partisanship for them and for lineages. Similar to this is zealous adherence to schools of thought, methods, and shaykhs, preferring some over others out of whim and partisanship, being affiliated with them, calling to them, allying with and opposing on their basis, and weighing people by them. All of this is from the calls of the *Jahiliyyah*.

Among them: calling the night prayer *'atamah* so predominantly that the word *'isha'* is abandoned.

Among them: the prohibition of reviling a Muslim, of two people conversing privately to the exclusion of a third, and of a woman describing the beauty of another woman to her husband.

Among them: saying in supplication, "O God, forgive me if You will, and have mercy on me if You will."

Among them: excessive swearing of oaths.

Among them: disliking the saying "*Qawsu Quzah*" (rainbow) for what appears in the sky.

Among them: asking someone by the Face of God.

Among them: calling Medina "Yathrib."

Among them: asking a man why he beat his wife, unless there is a need for that.

Among them: saying, "I fasted the whole of Ramadan," or "I stood in prayer the whole night."

**Section**

Among the disliked expressions is the explicit mention of things that should be referred to by euphemism rather than by their plain names.

Among them: saying, "May God prolong your life, perpetuate your days, and may you live a thousand years," and the like.

Among them: a fasting person saying, "By the One whose seal is upon the mouth of the unbeliever."

Among them: calling unjust taxes "rights" (*huquq*). And saying of what one spends in obedience to God, "I was made to pay a debt" or "I lost such-and-such," and saying, "I spent much wealth in this world."

Among them: a mufti saying, "God has made such-and-such lawful, and God has made such-and-such unlawful," regarding matters of *ijtihad* (independent legal reasoning). He should say this only regarding what a text has explicitly forbidden.

Among them: calling the proofs of the Qur'an and Sunnah "apparent verbal meanings" and "metaphors." This naming removes their sanctity from hearts, especially when one adds to it the naming of the doubts of the theologians and philosophers as "rational certainties." "There is no god but God": how much corruption in minds, in religions, in worldly life and in faith has resulted from these two namings.

Among them: a man narrating his intercourse with his wife and what takes place between him and her, as the lowly do.

Among what is disliked of expressions: "they claimed," "they mentioned," "they said," and the like.

Among what is disliked: saying to the sultan, "Caliph of God" or "Deputy of God on His earth." The caliph and the deputy are only of one who is absent, whereas God, glorified and exalted, is the caliph of the absent over his household, and the trustee of His believing servant.

**(Section)**

Let him be utterly wary of the transgression of "I" (*ana*), "mine" (*li*), and "with me" (*'indi*).

For these three expressions were the trial of Iblis, Pharaoh, and Qarun: "(I am better than him)" for Iblis, ﴿The kingdom of Egypt is mine﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 51] for Pharaoh, and ﴿I was only given it on knowledge I have﴾ [Al-Qasas: 78] for Qarun.

The best placement of "I" is in the servant's saying: "I am the servant who sins, who errs, who seeks forgiveness, who acknowledges," and the like. "Mine" is in his saying: "Mine is the sin, mine is the crime, mine is the humility and the poverty and the humiliation." "With me" is in his saying: "Forgive me my seriousness and my jesting, my error and my intention, for all of that is with me."

(Qā'ida)

The one who seeks Allah and the Last Abode cannot have his journey and his seeking set right except through two kinds of restraint: restraining his heart in its seeking and in what it seeks, and restraining it from turning to anything else; restraining his tongue from what is of no benefit and holding it to the remembrance of Allah and to what increases his faith and knowledge; and restraining his limbs from sins and desires and holding them to what is obligatory and recommended. He does not leave this restraint until he meets his Lord, who then frees him from the prison into the widest and most pleasant expanse. But whoever does not endure these two restraints and flees from them into the expanse of desires, that dreadful restraint will follow him when he departs from this world. So every one who leaves this world is either freed from restraint or going toward restraint. And success is from Allah.

(Faṣl)

The root of all blameworthy character traits is arrogance, humiliation and baseness, and the root of all praiseworthy character traits is humility (khushū') and loftiness of aspiration (ʿulūw al-himma). Boasting (fakhr), exultation (baṭar), insolence (ashar), self-admiration (ʿujb), envy (ḥasad), tyranny (baghy), conceit (khuyalā'), injustice (ẓulm), harshness (qaswa), domineering (tajabbur), aversion (i'rāḍ), refusal to accept advice (ibā' qubūl al-naṣīḥa), selfishness (istithār), seeking exaltation, loving status and leadership, wishing to be praised for what one did not do, and similar things, all arise from arrogance. As for lying, meanness, treachery, showing off (riyā'), deceit, trickery, greed, fear, cowardice, stinginess, incapacity, laziness, abasement before other than Allah, exchanging what is lower for what is better, and the like, these stem from humiliation, baseness and smallness of soul.

As for virtuous character traits, such as patience (ṣabr), courage (shajā'a), justice ('adl), manliness (murū'a), chastity (ʿiffa), self-protection (ṣiyāna), generosity (jūd), forbearance (ḥilm), pardon (ʿafw), forgiveness (ṣafḥ), tolerance (iḥtimāl), preferring others (īthār), self-respect that keeps one from base things (ʿizzat al-nafs ʿan al-danāʾāt), humility (tawāḍuʿ), contentment (qanāʿa), truthfulness (ṣidq), good manners (akhlāq), repaying kindness with its like or better, overlooking people's slips (taghāful), leaving off what does not concern one (tark al-infighāl bimā lā yaʿnīhi), and the soundness of the heart from those blameworthy traits, and the like, all of them arise from humility and loftiness of aspiration. Allah, glorified is He, informed about the earth that it becomes humble (khāshiʿa), then water is sent down upon it, and it stirs, swells, and takes on its adornment and splendor. Likewise is the one created from it, when his share of success reaches him.

As for fire, its nature is elevation and corruption, then it subsides and becomes the lowliest and most abased thing. Likewise is the one created from it: he is always between elevation when it is roused and agitated, and baseness and lowliness when it subsides and calms. Blameworthy character traits follow fire and what is created from it, and virtuous character traits follow earth and what is created from it. Whoever's aspiration is lofty and whose soul is humble is characterized by every beautiful trait, and whoever's aspiration is low and whose soul is insolent is characterized by every vile trait.

**[Section: Defining the Murad]**

The author of *al-Manazil* said:

*Chapter on the Murad (the one who is willed). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿You did not expect that the Book would be sent down to you, except as a mercy from your Lord﴾.*

Most of those who spoke on this science treated the murid (the one who wills, the seeker) and the murad (the one who is willed, the chosen) as two, and they placed the station of the murad above the station of the murid. By the name murad they indicated the cherished ones (al-dana'in) about whom a report has come.

I say: The way he cites the verse as evidence is that Allah, glorified is He, cast His Book upon His Messenger, singled him out with His honour, and qualified him for his mission and prophethood, without this being on his own hope, or his having attained it through earning, or his having sought it through any deed. Rather, it is a matter that was willed for him. Thus he is the murad in truth.

As for his saying that most of them treated the murid and the murad as two, it is an allusion that some of them dispensed with mentioning the station of the murad, considering the station of willing (al-iradah) sufficient, because its holder is both a murid and a murad.

He illustrated the murid and the murad with a people whom a king summoned to his court from distant lands. He sent them proofs, wealth, mounts, and all kinds of provisions, and ordered them to endure the crossing of roads and deserts and to strive in their journey until they reached him. He then sent his own horses and slaves to a group among them, and said: "Mount them on these horses that outpace the riding beasts, serve them on their way, do not let them suffer the burden of tying and fastening, and when they halt, give them rest. Then carry them until you bring them before me."

Those people did not experience the exertion of the journey, its hardship, or the toil of travel as the others did.

Some people say: The murid moves from the station of willing until he becomes a murad, so he was a lover (muhibb) and became one who is loved (mahbub). Thus every sincere murid's ultimate end is to become a murad, and most of them hold this view.

It seems that the author of *al-Manazil* means by the murad the one who is drawn (al-majdhub), and by the murid the wayfarer (al-salik) on the main path.

**[Degrees of the Murad]**

**[Section: The First Degree is that He Protects the Servant]**

He said: The murad has three degrees. The first: that He protects the servant. He is poised for estrangement, compelled by the embittering of desires, the obstructing of pleasures, and the blocking of the paths of ruin against him, by force.

Meaning: When the servant's soul inclines toward estrangement between himself and his Master, by following his desires, his Master protects him by compulsion, by embittering his desires for him, so that they are never pure for him. Rather, he attains only some of them mixed with kinds of embitterment, which may outweigh their pleasure and consume it, so that pleasure in comparison with the embitterment is like a stolen moment or a moment of heedlessness. Likewise He obstructs pleasures from him by standing between him and them, so that he does not incline to them, nor feel at ease with them and dwell in them. Thus He stands between him and their causes.

If they are made available to him, an opponent is appointed to stand between him and enjoying them, and he says: "From where have you been struck?" For this is the eye of care, protection, and safeguarding.

Likewise He closes off from him the paths of sins, for they are the paths of ruin, even if he dislikes it, out of care for him and protection of him.

**[Section: The Second Degree is that He Lifts from the Servant the Accidents of Deficiency]**

He said: The second degree is that He lifts from the servant the accidents of deficiency, preserves him from the mark of blame, and grants him ownership over the consequences of lapses.

As He did with Sulayman, peace be upon him, when he slew the horses, and so He carried him on the gentle wind and made him independent of the horses. And He did with Musa, peace be upon him, when he threw down the tablets and seized his brother by the head, and He did not rebuke him as He rebuked Adam, peace be upon him, and Nuh, Dawud, and Yunus, peace be upon them all.

The difference between this degree and the one before it is that in the previous one there is a prevention from engaging in the causes of estrangement, by compulsion.

In this one, when causes of deficiency arise for him, for which he deserves blame, He does not reproach him for them nor blame him.

This is a kind of intimacy (dalal), and its holder is among the cherished ones and beloved of Allah. For the beloved is forgiving in what he does not forgive in others, because love is the greatest of his intercessors. When he commits a lapse, He grants him ownership of its consequence, by making it a cause for his elevation and the lifting of his rank. So that lapse becomes a cause for sincere repentance (tawbah nasuh), specific humility, and brokenness before Him, and righteous deeds that increase his nearness to Him many times over what he had before the lapse. Thus that lapse is more beneficial to him than many good deeds. This is among the signs of Allah's care for the servant and of his being among His beloved and His party.

The Shaykh (al-Harawi) cited the story of Sulayman, peace be upon him, when the horses distracted him from the afternoon prayer. He was seized by anger for Allah and zeal, so he went on to wipe their hamstrings and necks with the sword, and destroyed property that had preoccupied him from Allah, for the sake of Allah.

So Allah compensated him for it by carrying him upon the back of the wind. Allah granted him ownership of the consequence of this lapse and made it a cause for attaining that exalted station.

He also cited the story of Musa, peace be upon him, when he threw down the tablets, in which was the speech of Allah, seized his brother's head, broke them, and dragged him by the beard. He was a prophet like him, and Allah did not rebuke him for that, whereas He rebuked Adam, peace be upon him, for eating a morsel from the tree, and Nuh concerning his son when he asked his Lord to save him, and Dawud regarding the matter of the wife of Uriyah.

And [He rebuked] Yunus regarding the matter of his leaving in anger.

I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, say: Likewise Musa struck the eye of the Angel of Death and gouged it out, and his Lord did not rebuke him for it. On the night of the Isra' he [Musa] rebuked his Lord concerning the Prophet (ﷺ), since He had elevated him above him, and he raised his voice about that, yet Allah did not rebuke him for it. He said: Because Musa, peace be upon him, performed those great stations which made this intimacy (dalal) due to him. For he opposed Pharaoh, the greatest enemy of Allah, confronted him and his people, dealt with the Children of Israel in the most severe manner, strove for Allah against the enemies of Allah with the most intense striving, and was extremely zealous for his Lord, so He tolerated from him what He did not tolerate from others.

As for Dhu al-Nun, when he was not in this station, He imprisoned him in the belly of the fish for his anger, and Allah has set a measure for everything.

**[Section: The Third Degree is the Choosing of the Servant by the Real]**

He said: The third degree: the choosing (ijtiba') of the servant by the Real, and His selecting him for Himself with His own purity, as He began with Musa, when he went out seeking a fire, and He chose him for Himself and left of him a borrowed trace.

I say: *Ijtiba'* means election, preference, and specification. It is an *iftiʿal* form derived from *jabaytu al-shay'*, when you gather a thing and bring it to yourself, like the collection of taxes and other things.

*Istina'* (making for oneself, favouring) also means election and choosing. The meaning is that He chose Musa and selected him for Himself, and made him purely His own, without any cause from Musa and without any means. For he went out to seek fire, and returned as the one who speaks with the Single, the Subduer, and the most honoured of creation in His sight, beginning from Him, glorified is He, without any prior claim to merit and without any preceding means. In this regard it has been said:

*O servant, be for what you do not hope for,*
*of goodness, more hopeful than what you are hoping for.*

*Indeed Musa came seeking a fire*
*from a light he saw, while the night was dark.*

*So he turned back, and Allah had spoken to him,*
*and He conversed with him, and He is the best of interlocutors.*

As for his saying: "and left of him a borrowed trace":

It may be that by the trace he means the remainder through which Muhammad (ﷺ) preceded him, and he was raised above him by degrees because of its remaining in him.

It may also be (and this is the more apparent) that He took him from himself, made him for Himself, chose him from among the worlds, singled him out with His speech, and left for him of his own self only a bare trace by which he accompanies creation, and upon which the rulings of humanity apply, to complete His wisdom and manifest His power. So it is a loan with Him. When He has fulfilled what is upon him, He reclaims that trace, makes it of His own property, and then the station of choosing is perfected, outwardly and inwardly, in reality and in trace, and the loan returns to its true owner, to whom the whole affair returns. Thus, as it began from Him, it returns to Him.

Musa, peace be upon him, was in the manifestation of majesty, and for this reason his law was a law of majesty and subjugation. They were commanded to kill themselves, fats and animals with claws and other good things were forbidden to them, spoils were forbidden to them, punishments were hastened upon them as they were, and they were burdened with heavy duties and shackles that no one else carried.

Musa (ﷺ) was among the greatest of Allah's creation in awe and dignity, and the most severe of them in might and zeal for Allah, and in seizing the enemies of Allah. None could look at him steadily.

'Isa (ﷺ) was in the manifestation of beauty. His law was a law of grace and kindness. He did not fight nor wage war, and there is no fighting at all in his law. The Christians' religion forbids them fighting, and they are disobedient to his law in this, for the Gospel commands them: "Whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the left. Whoever sues you for your garment, give him your cloak. Whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him two miles," and similar things. There is no hardship in their law, no heavy burdens, and no shackles. Rather the Christians themselves invented that monasticism, and it was not prescribed for them.

As for our Prophet (ﷺ): he was in the manifestation of perfection, combining that strength, justice, and severity for Allah, with this gentleness, tenderness, and mercy. His law is the most perfect of laws. He is the Prophet of perfection, and his law is the law of perfection. His community is the most perfect of nations, and their states and stations are the most perfect of states and stations. For this reason his law brings justice as an obligation and a duty, grace as a recommendation and a preference, severity in the place of severity, and gentleness in the place of gentleness.

The sword was placed in its place, and generosity was placed in its place. So [he] mentions injustice and prohibits it, and justice and makes it obligatory, and grace and recommends it, in some verses.

Like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾, which is justice. ﴿But whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah﴾, which is grace. ﴿Indeed He does not love the wrongdoers﴾, which is the prohibition of injustice.

And His saying: ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of what you were punished with﴾, which is an obligation of justice and a prohibition of injustice. ﴿But if you are patient, it is better for the patient﴾, which recommends grace.

And His saying: ﴿And if you repent, then for you is the principal of your wealth; you do not wrong and you are not wronged﴾, which is a prohibition of injustice. ﴿And if one is in difficulty, then let there be postponement until a time of ease﴾, which is justice. ﴿And that you give charity is better for you, if you knew﴾, which is grace.

Likewise, the prohibition of what He forbade to his community is for protection and safeguarding. He forbade them every filthy and harmful thing, and permitted them every good and beneficial thing. So His prohibiting it to them is mercy, while for those before them there was not free of punishment.

He guided them to what the nations before them had strayed from, and He bestowed upon them of His knowledge and forbearance.

He made them the best community brought forth for mankind, and perfected for them of excellences what He had dispersed among the nations before them.

Just as He perfected for their Prophet (ﷺ) of excellences what He had dispersed among the prophets before him.

And He perfected in His Book of excellences what He had dispersed among the books before it. Likewise in His law.

These, then, are the cherished ones, and they are the chosen and the best, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He has chosen you, and has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion﴾ [al-Hajj: 78]. He made them witnesses over mankind, and established them in this station as the prophets were witnesses over their nations.

The detailed account of the excellence of this community and its distinctive features calls for a book, indeed books.

That is the bounty of Allah, He gives it to whom He wills, and Allah is the Owner of great bounty.
